title: Preparing a spacious enclosure
steps: Choose a large single-level enclosure with ample floor space for running and exploring.
Add hideaways, hay stations, water and comfortable dry bedding.
caution: Small pet-shop cages are often too small for permanent housing.

title: Why guinea pigs need companions
steps: Plan to keep guinea pigs with compatible guinea pig companions rather than alone.
Introduce new animals carefully in a neutral, spacious area with multiple hiding places.
caution: Never house guinea pigs with rabbits; their needs and communication differ.

title: Choosing compatible companions
steps: Consider established pairs or groups with suitable sex and temperament combinations.
Provide several feeding areas and shelters with two exits to reduce guarding.
caution: Check sexes carefully; mixed-sex groups can breed unless appropriately neutered.

title: Settling in a new guinea pig
steps: Set up the enclosure before arrival with hay, water and familiar food.
Give the guinea pig quiet time and let it approach you at its own pace.
caution: Avoid forced handling during the settling-in period.

title: Daily health observation
steps: Watch eating, drinking, droppings, movement and normal interactions each day.
Check eyes, nose, coat and posture for changes from the animal's usual behaviour.
caution: A guinea pig that stops eating or passing droppings needs urgent veterinary advice.

title: Unlimited grass hay
steps: Offer a constant supply of clean, good-quality grass hay such as timothy or meadow hay.
Replace damp or soiled hay and make it easy to reach from several spots.
caution: Hay supports gut movement and tooth wear; do not substitute seed mixes.

title: Vitamin C every day
steps: Provide fresh guinea-pig-appropriate vegetables rich in vitamin C and a suitable fortified pellet.
Refresh food daily and store pellets according to packaging guidance.
caution: Guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C; ask a vet about supplementation if intake is uncertain.

title: Choosing suitable pellets
steps: Use a plain, guinea-pig-specific fortified pellet in the amount recommended for your pets.
Check expiry dates and keep pellets dry in a sealed container.
caution: Avoid colourful muesli mixes that encourage selective feeding.

title: Introducing new vegetables
steps: Offer one new safe vegetable in a small amount alongside the usual diet.
Observe appetite and droppings before increasing the amount gradually.
caution: Sudden diet changes may upset digestion.

title: Safe leafy greens
steps: Offer a varied selection of guinea-pig-safe leafy greens washed and served fresh.
Rotate suitable greens and remove uneaten pieces before they spoil.
caution: Some greens are high in calcium; ask your vet about diet if urinary problems occur.

title: Bell peppers as vitamin C food
steps: Wash a fresh bell pepper and offer a suitable portion with seeds and stalk removed.
Combine with hay, suitable pellets and other safe greens.
caution: Vegetables complement rather than replace hay.

title: Fruit as an occasional treat
steps: Offer a tiny piece of suitable fruit only occasionally.
Remove uneaten fruit promptly to prevent spoilage and insects.
caution: Fruit is sugary and should not form a routine large portion of the diet.

title: Foods to avoid
steps: Keep chocolate, onion, garlic, avocado and human snack foods out of reach.
Check unfamiliar plants or foods with a reliable veterinary source before offering.
caution: Contact a vet promptly if a potentially toxic item has been eaten.

title: Fresh drinking water
steps: Provide clean drinking water in a stable bowl or a working bottle, depending on what your guinea pigs use reliably.
Wash containers and check water flow every day.
caution: Seek veterinary advice if drinking changes markedly.

title: Monitoring body weight
steps: Weigh each guinea pig using a digital kitchen scale and a secure container.
Record the weight and compare it with previous measurements.
caution: Unexplained weight loss can be an early illness sign even when the guinea pig looks normal.

title: Understanding normal droppings
steps: Notice the usual number, shape and consistency of droppings during daily cleaning.
Keep a record if droppings become smaller, fewer or unusually soft.
caution: No droppings or reduced eating is urgent; do not wait overnight.

title: Recognising dental problems
steps: Watch for slow eating, dropping food, wet chin, weight loss or reluctance to chew hay.
Arrange prompt examination by a guinea-pig-experienced vet if signs appear.
caution: Back teeth cannot be assessed properly at home; do not attempt trimming.

title: Signs of respiratory illness
steps: Look for noisy breathing, nasal discharge, crusty eyes, lethargy or reduced appetite.
Keep the guinea pig calm and contact a vet promptly if symptoms appear.
caution: Breathing difficulty is an emergency; avoid human cold medicines.

title: Skin and fungal concerns
steps: Check for bald patches, scabs, itching and changes in the skin during routine handling.
Use clean bedding and seek veterinary identification of the cause.
caution: Some fungal infections can spread to people; wash hands and avoid home remedies.

title: Mites and lice awareness
steps: Watch for intense scratching, flaky skin, hair loss or discomfort.
Ask a vet to identify parasites and recommend species-safe treatment.
caution: Never use dog or cat flea products without explicit veterinary instruction.

title: Bumblefoot prevention
steps: Provide dry, soft, solid flooring and inspect feet gently for redness or swelling.
Keep nails trimmed and maintain a healthy weight and clean enclosure.
caution: Sores or limping require veterinary care.

title: Urinary discomfort signs
steps: Notice squeaking during urination, straining, blood or wetness around the rear.
Record symptoms and arrange a veterinary examination promptly.
caution: Straining or inability to pass urine is urgent.

title: Heat stress prevention
steps: Place housing in a cool, ventilated area away from direct sun and hot windows.
Offer shade, cool drinking water and a wrapped cool pack with space to move away.
caution: Panting, collapse or severe lethargy in heat is an emergency.

title: Cold weather protection
steps: Keep guinea pigs in a dry, draught-free environment with suitable bedding and shelter.
Check temperatures and avoid sudden moves between extreme indoor and outdoor conditions.
caution: Guinea pigs are sensitive to cold and damp conditions.

title: Outdoor grazing safely
steps: Use a secure covered run on untreated grass with shade, hiding places and water.
Supervise and check for poisonous plants, pesticides and predators.
caution: Never leave guinea pigs exposed to direct sun or unsupervised outdoors.

title: Predator-proof housing
steps: Check mesh, doors, latches and the floor or base for weak points.
Ensure cats, dogs, foxes and birds of prey cannot reach the animals.
caution: A nearby predator can frighten guinea pigs even without direct contact.

title: Choosing safe bedding
steps: Use absorbent, low-dust bedding or washable fleece with an appropriate absorbent layer.
Keep resting areas dry and change damp sections promptly.
caution: Avoid strongly scented or dusty materials that may irritate breathing.

title: Spot-cleaning the enclosure
steps: Remove wet bedding, leftover vegetables and heavily soiled hay.
Top up fresh hay and check water and hiding areas.
caution: Avoid leaving guinea pigs in a wet enclosure.

title: Full enclosure cleaning
steps: Move guinea pigs to a secure temporary area with hay and water.
Clean and dry the enclosure using pet-safe products before replacing bedding.
caution: Rinse away cleaner residue and never mix cleaning chemicals.

title: Hiding places with exits
steps: Provide at least one comfortable hide per guinea pig, plus an extra if space permits.
Choose shelters with more than one exit so no animal can be trapped.
caution: Avoid sharp edges and overcrowded hideouts.

title: Tunnels and enrichment
steps: Offer safe cardboard tunnels, paper bags with handles removed and hay-filled activities.
Rotate items and allow guinea pigs to investigate at their own pace.
caution: Remove damaged plastic or chew hazards.

title: Floor time indoors
steps: Set up a guinea-pig-proof exercise area with hides, hay and water.
Supervise and block cables, gaps and unsafe furniture access.
caution: Never use exercise balls or running wheels for guinea pigs.

title: Safe handling and lifting
steps: Approach calmly, support the chest and hindquarters, and lift close to your body.
Sit low to the floor while holding a guinea pig to reduce injury risk.
caution: Never lift by legs, ears or scruff.

title: Helping shy guinea pigs trust you
steps: Sit near the enclosure and speak quietly while offering safe food by hand.
Let the guinea pig choose to approach and keep sessions short.
caution: Avoid chasing or grabbing frightened animals.

title: Understanding wheeks and purrs
steps: Observe vocalisations alongside posture and context, such as food anticipation or relaxation.
Learn each guinea pig's normal communication over time.
caution: Teeth chattering and stiff postures can signal tension.

title: Recognising social tension
steps: Watch for persistent chasing, biting, blocked access to food or one animal hiding constantly.
Provide more space, hay stations and shelters with two exits.
caution: Separate safely and seek experienced advice if injuries or serious fighting occur.

title: Nail trimming basics
steps: Inspect nail length regularly and use suitable small-animal clippers if confident.
Trim only the tip, avoiding the quick, or ask a vet nurse to demonstrate.
caution: Dark nails can make the quick hard to see; do not cut blindly.

title: Brushing long-haired guinea pigs
steps: Gently comb long hair to remove tangles and prevent soiling.
Check around the rear and underside for mats and trapped debris.
caution: Do not pull painful mats; ask a professional or vet for help.

title: Bathing only when necessary
steps: Use spot-cleaning where possible rather than routine full baths.
Ask a vet for advice if coat contamination or skin problems make bathing necessary.
caution: Guinea pigs chill easily; never use human shampoo or leave them damp.

title: Checking the rear end
steps: Look for dampness, faecal buildup, soiled fur or skin irritation around the rear.
Clean minor surface dirt gently and investigate repeated soiling.
caution: Flystrike or maggots are an emergency requiring immediate veterinary care.

title: Travelling to the vet
steps: Use a secure ventilated carrier lined with absorbent bedding and hay.
Keep the carrier stable, shaded and away from temperature extremes.
caution: Never leave guinea pigs in a parked car.

title: Finding an experienced vet
steps: Locate a veterinary practice experienced with guinea pigs before an emergency.
Keep the phone number and out-of-hours details accessible.
caution: Not all veterinary practices routinely treat small mammals.

title: Quarantine and introductions
steps: Discuss quarantine and health checks with a vet or rescue before mixing new guinea pigs.
Introduce compatible animals in a spacious neutral area under supervision.
caution: Do not rush introductions or ignore aggressive behaviour.

title: Caring for older guinea pigs
steps: Make hay, food, water and hiding places easy to access without climbing.
Monitor weight, mobility, grooming and appetite more closely.
caution: New stiffness, pain or weight changes need veterinary assessment.

title: Young guinea pig care
steps: Provide a secure enclosure, suitable age-appropriate feeding and gentle handling.
Ask a vet or experienced rescue about growth, sexing and safe grouping.
caution: Incorrect sexing can lead to unexpected pregnancies.

title: Pregnancy prevention
steps: Confirm the sex of every guinea pig and keep unneutered males and females apart.
Discuss neutering and safe pairings with an experienced vet or rescue.
caution: Guinea pig pregnancy and birth can carry significant risks.

title: Keeping a care record
steps: Write down weights, diet changes, vet visits and medication instructions.
Update notes after health checks or unusual symptoms.
caution: Records help a vet spot patterns but do not replace examination.

title: Emergency appetite checklist
steps: If a guinea pig eats less, check hay intake, droppings, posture and activity immediately.
Contact an experienced vet urgently rather than waiting for the next day.
caution: Do not force-feed an unwell guinea pig unless a vet directs you.

title: Safe household plants
steps: Keep houseplants and cut flowers out of reach of curious guinea pigs.
Verify any plants used near grazing or exercise areas are safe.
caution: Many ornamental plants are toxic; seek veterinary advice after suspected ingestion.

title: Children and guinea pigs
steps: Teach children to speak softly and interact while sitting on the floor.
Have an adult supervise handling, feeding and enclosure access.
caution: Guinea pigs can be injured by falls or rough handling.
